chunks: Why SPI is faster than I2C. The question: Which is faster? Why?
SPI is faster than I2C for two reasons.
First, SPI drives its wires hard in both directions, while I2C drives a wire down firmly but lets a resistor pull it back up, and that climb is slow.
Second, I2C carries more extra bits around each byte: an address and a confirmation bit. Together these let SPI run at tens of MHz, while I2C tops out near 1 megahertz.
Picture a bucket whose water level is the wire's voltage. A big drain empties it fast, which is a device pulling the wire low.
I2C refills it through a thin hose, the pull-up resistor, so the level creeps up slowly. SPI has both a big drain and a big hose, so it fills and empties fast.
A thicker hose helps, but it wastes more water whenever the drain is open.
When the device's switch is closed it pulls the line low quickly (a transistor, ohms).
When it opens, only R p is left to charge C b , so the rise is an exponential with time constant R pC b .
The fall is fast, the rise is slow, which is why I2C waveforms look asymmetric.
Push-pull: an output that actively drives the wire both high and low. SPI uses it. Open-drain: an output that can only pull the wire low.
I2C uses it ("Advantages of open-drain outputs"). Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts an I2C wire to high ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Bus capacitance: the electrical "bucket size" of the wires, pins and traces that must be charged ("What is I2C bus capacitance").
Rise time: how long a signal takes to climb from low to high. Overhead: bits on the wire that are not data, such as the address and confirmation bits.
A good estimate is that the rise time is about 0. 85 times R times C . An I2C bus with a 4. 7 kilohms pull-up and 100 picofarads of capacitance gives 0.
85 times 4700 times 100 picofarads about 400 nanoseconds (billionths of a second). The limit for 400 kilohertz mode is 300 nanoseconds, so this is too slow.
An SPI output with about 30 ohms on the same capacitance gives roughly 2. 5 nanoseconds. That is the whole idea.
"SPI is faster for two reasons. First, its push-pull outputs drive both edges hard, so you can clock at tens of MHz. I2C's rising edge is an RC charge through a pull-up, about 0.
85 R pC b , which caps it around 100 kilohertz to 1 megahertz. Second, I2C has more overhead: 9 clocks per byte plus an address and often a register byte.
So a 14-byte read is roughly 380 microseconds on 400 kilohertz I2C versus 12 microseconds on 10 megahertz SPI."
